summary: Analyzes security threats to Multipath TCP, which lets one connection use several paths, and what is needed to keep it as secure as regular TCP. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Using several roads at once opens more ways for a bad guy to interfere. This lists the dangers.

questions: what are the security threats to multipath tcp
what is a flooding attack in mptcp
why do nats make mptcp security hard
subtitle: What new attacks appear when a TCP connection can use several addresses, and what to do about them.

tldr.problem: Letting each end of a TCP connection use more than one IP address could make Multipath TCP (MPTCP) less secure than regular TCP, even against attackers who are not on the path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC studies two attack families, flooding and hijacking, including time-shifted hijacking and the effect of NATs, and then recommends defenses for the MPTCP design.
tldr.outcome: It recommends a reachability check with a random nonce before adding an address, plus a keyed HMAC based on a key exchanged in the first subflow, so MPTCP is as secure as current TCP.

today: RFC 6181 is Informational and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It was written as input for the MPTCP designers, and the companion architecture is in RFC 6182.

sections.title: Scope of the Analysis
sections.content:
This RFC looks only at the multi-addressed flavor of Multipath TCP, where different source-destination address pairs express different paths. It covers only the additional vulnerabilities compared with single-path TCP. The goal is an MPTCP that is as secure as current TCP, not more secure.

On-path attackers can already eavesdrop and hijack in plain TCP, so they are out of scope. Off-path attackers and time-shifted attackers, who are on the path briefly and then move away, are in scope.

The RFC compares the problem with Mobile IPv6 route optimization, Shim6 and SCTP, and concludes MPTCP still needs its own analysis. One example: in MPTCP an added address affects only one connection, so less is at stake.
sections.plainLanguage: The note only worries about new tricks that come from having many roads. Tricks that already work on a single road are somebody else's problem.

sections.title: Assumptions About a Basic MPTCP
sections.content:
Because no MPTCP specification existed to analyze, the RFC assumes only the basics. A connection starts with the TCP 3-way handshake on one address pair, uses a single data sequence number space, and is identified by the 4-tuple of source address, source port, destination address and destination port.

Addresses are then added by a control message in one of two modes. In explicit mode the message lists addresses. In implicit mode the address added is the source address of the IP header, which may benefit from ingress filtering. The explicit mode seems more vulnerable to abuse, and the RFC warns against relying on ingress filtering because deployment is far from universal.

MPTCP also changes the trust model slightly: the initiator trusts the peer to supply extra addresses it will trust as much as the original pair.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection begins on one road. Later either side can say "you can also reach me at this other address," either by writing it down or by just using it.

sections.title: Flooding Attacks
sections.content:
In a flooding (bombing) attack, an attacker A starts a large download from a server S over MPTCP, then adds the victim T's address IPT as one of its own addresses. By pretending the path to IPT is fine and the path to A's real address is congested, A makes S send the download to T. S believes it is still talking to A. T replies with RST packets, but a window grown beforehand can still produce a lot of traffic. Coupled congestion windows, or slow start per subflow, may limit the damage.

A second flooding attack uses explicit mode: the attacker sends a long list of addresses in one packet, and a peer that opens subflows to all of them is amplified into sending to every destination.

MIPv6 route optimization and SCTP handle this with a reachability check before using a new address, usually with a nonce the attacker cannot guess. SCTP uses a 64-bit nonce in a HEARTBEAT. A 3-way handshake on each new address pair would work as that check.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster asks a delivery truck to also deliver to an innocent neighbor's house, and the neighbor gets buried in boxes. The fix is for the truck to knock on the neighbor's door first.

sections.title: Hijacking and Time-Shifted Attacks
sections.content:
In a hijacking attack, the attacker adds its own address IPA to a connection between Node 1 and Node 2. It needs the 4-tuple, and the client port is the hard part to learn. Node 2 then sends part of the data to the attacker, which already acts as a DoS since the byte stream stalls waiting for missing data. By removing IP1 from the address set, the attacker can take over the whole flow. Adding itself at both ends makes a MiTM attack.

A cookie sent in plaintext at setup stops off-path attackers but not time-shifted ones, who sniff the cookie while on the path and use it later. The RFC compares three approaches:

  • Cookie: any sniffed control message reveals it, and endpoints cannot detect misuse.
  • Shared secret in plaintext plus HMAC: the secret is exposed only in the first subflow exchange, but the HMAC cannot cover the added IP address, so the address can still be altered.
  • Strong crypto anchor (public key or hash chain anchor): the forgery window is only the initial exchange, and the attack is detectable if the endpoints talk directly.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person adds themselves to your phone call. Using a secret password helps, but if they peeked at it once, they can come back later.

sections.title: NATs and Integrity Protection
sections.content:
To be widely adopted, MPTCP must work through NATs, and a NAT acts much like a MiTM attacker because it rewrites addresses. So MPTCP must accept NAT-rewritten addresses, which means implicit-mode messages (the SYN of a new subflow) cannot have integrity protection over the address. The RFC says it is far from obvious what a creative alternative would look like.

In explicit mode the address in the option could be protected, but if the host is behind a NAT, its configured address is unreachable and useless. NAT traversal techniques such as STUN could learn the mapped address, but that relies on extra tools.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail room that rewrites the return address on every letter makes it hard to tell real senders from fakes.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
After weighing the trade-off between solution complexity and leftover threats, the MPTCP working group concluded that:

  • MPTCP should do a reachability check using a random nonce (for example a TCP 3-way handshake) before adding a new address, to prevent flooding.
  • The default mechanism should exchange a key in cleartext in the first subflow, then protect later address additions with a keyed HMAC.
  • It should also support a pre-shared key for the HMAC, for stronger protection.
  • It should provide replay protection, for example an HMAC-protected sequence number.
  • MPTCP should be extensible to accommodate more secure mechanisms later.

The Security Considerations section says only that the note itself is a security analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Knock on the new door first, share a secret handshake, and make every message fresh so it cannot be replayed.
